title: Venture capital investments in artificial intelligence through 2025
authors: OECD
institution: OECD (Policy Briefs No. 50)
verification: Abstract and publication metadata (DOI 10.1787/a13752f5-en, 16 pages, dated 17 February 2026) read at origin via full-page capture 2026-11-05; underlying Preqin data not accessed.
relevance: The OECD's data-based tracking of global venture capital into AI firms through 2025, drawing on Preqin data curated at the OECD.AI Policy Observatory — an official, cross-country dataset complementing US-centric trackers. The brief outlines policy actions to foster enabling investment environments, strengthen domestic AI ecosystems, and support trustworthy AI innovation across the technology stack. Useful for mapping where AI startup funding flows by country and funding stage, with the caveat that the landing-page abstract does not quantify totals.

title: Government as Venture Capitalists in AI
authors: Martin Beraja, Wenwei Peng, David Y. Yang, Noam Yuchtman
institution: NBER (Working Paper 32701)
verification: Abstract read at origin (nber.org) 2026-11-05. A published version appears in Entrepreneurship and Innovation Policy and the Economy, volume 4 (2025), per the NBER page.
relevance: Studies China's government venture capital funds in AI, where national and local governments act as VCs, using comprehensive data on Chinese government and private VC funds. The authors find government funds are distributed more widely across space than private funds and back firms with weaker pre-investment performance signals — yet those firms grow faster than private-VC-backed firms. Private VC funds tend to invest after government VCs, especially when a firm's hometown government fund makes direct investments in weaker-signal firms. Read through the lens of VC's role in overcoming information frictions under China's institutional constraints; a rare large-scale dataset on state-directed AI investment.

title: Financing the AI Buildout
authors: Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh
institution: NBER (Working Paper 35865); forthcoming Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, Fall 2026
verification: Abstract read at origin (nber.org) 2026-11-05; full paper not read. Issue date October 2026 per NBER page.
relevance: Sizes and maps the financing of AI infrastructure: the abstract estimates a 1 GW AI campus costs roughly $41 billion and that completing a 188 GW US buildout by 2032 would require nearly $9 trillion of total investment, equal to annual investment of about 3.2 percent of GDP over 2025-2032. As hyperscaler capital expenditures exceed internal cash flow, financing shifts toward leases, joint ventures, project debt, private credit, securitization and special-purpose vehicles, which broaden capacity but raise asset-level leverage and obscure contingent obligations. The author flags tenant concentration, technological obsolescence, execution delays and uncertain residual values as risks. A finance-oriented companion to capex-discussion sources.

title: What unprecedented AI capex means for markets and investors
authors: J.P. Morgan Global Research (contributors: Michael Feroli, Dubravko Lakos-Bujas, Fabio Bassi, Harlan Sur, Tarek Hamid, Hannah Lee, Adrian Huerta)
institution: J.P. Morgan Global Research
verification: Full piece read at origin (jpmorgan.com) 2026-11-05.
relevance: An earnings-based synthesis of hyperscaler capital expenditure: J.P. Morgan revised its 2026 estimate for the five US hyperscalers (Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Oracle, Microsoft) up from $736 billion to $900 billion after mid-year earnings, projecting $5.5 trillion of cumulative AI capex by 2030. Using company filings through August 2026, it documents cloud revenue as early return on investment (AWS +37% year-on-year with a $496 billion backlog; Azure +43%; Google Cloud +82% with $514 billion backlog; Oracle cloud revenue rising from $2.1 billion in Q1 2025 to $5.8 billion in Q4 2026) and a financing shift from free cash flow to debt and equity, including Alphabet's $85 billion equity raise in June 2026. Bottlenecks cited include power (data centers at 9-17 percent of US electricity demand by 2030, up from 3-4 percent) and a DRAM shortage. Bank research, so figures reflect sell-side consensus revision practices rather than audited data.

title: World Trade Report 2025: Making trade and AI work together to the benefit of all
authors: World Trade Organization
institution: World Trade Organization
verification: Publication overview page read at origin (wto.org) 2026-11-05; full report not read. Launch news item dated 15 September 2025.
relevance: The WTO's flagship report on AI and international trade, launched 15 September 2025. It argues AI can cut trade costs, raise productivity and widen access to global markets, but that unequal access to digital infrastructure, skills and capabilities — plus AI's labour-market effects — could make benefits unevenly distributed, so policy design determines inclusiveness. Chapters cover the trade-AI relationship, domestic policies that shape it, and international cooperation, with the WTO's role framed as administering rules, fostering dialogue and transparency, and building capacity. The global-policy counterpart to empirical AI-trade papers.

title: Through the looking glass: artificial intelligence, international trade, and economic growth in the long run
authors: Eddy Bekkers, Lee Humphreys, Hryhorii Kalachyhin, Karolina Wilczynska, Danchen Zhao
institution: World Trade Organization (Staff Working Paper ERSD-2025-09)
verification: Abstract read at origin (wto.org) 2026-11-05; full paper not read.
relevance: Quantitative multi-sector, multi-factor trade model in which AI reallocates tasks from labour to AI services, raising productivity and cutting trade costs, with four scenarios varying how fast less-prepared economies catch up. In the most favourable scenario the authors project AI diffusion raises global GDP by an additional 13.2 percent over the next 15 years and global trade volumes 35 percent larger than without AI. Returns shift toward capital and the skill premium declines, though all factors gain in real terms. The authors caution the estimates are scenario-dependent and note low- and middle-income economies capture more gains with better digital infrastructure and broad AI deployment.

title: Artificial Intelligence and International Trade in Services: Evidence from the United States
authors: Paulo Bastos, Gaurav Nayyar
institution: World Bank (Development Research Group, draft supported by the Umbrella Facility for Trade trust fund)
verification: Abstract and introduction read from the PDF 2026-11-05; full 31-page draft not read.
relevance: First-pass causal evidence that AI adoption reshapes trade in services rather than only domestic jobs: using bilateral US services trade data for 2011-2024 with OLS and an IV strategy (occupational AI exposure interacted with nationwide AI adoption), the authors find US services sectors with stronger AI adoption increased exports more, to both developed and developing economies. They find no robust evidence that AI adoption reduces services imports, suggesting AI is not systematically replacing services sourced from other countries. Grounded in the Artuc-Bastos-Rijkers (2023) two-stage-production Ricardian model; limitations include the US-only setting and adoption measured by exposure proxies. Directly relevant to offshoring and outsourcing fears for developing-country service exporters.

title: Fairwork US Ratings 2025: When AI Eats the Manager
authors: Fairwork project, Oxford Internet Institute (University of Oxford); editorial contributors include Veena Dubal and Mark Graham
institution: Fairwork / Oxford Internet Institute, University of Oxford
verification: Publication page read at origin (fairwork.oii.ox.ac.uk) 2026-11-05; full report PDF (hosted under a 2025/03 path) not read. US companion to the Fairwork Latin America ratings already in the map.
relevance: The 2025 US edition of the Fairwork platform ratings takes AI-driven algorithmic management as its central theme, scoring major US platform and on-demand firms against fair-work principles. The report documents chatbots standing in for most forms of human management in ride-hail and delivery (handling pay disputes, shift cancellations and emergency support), algorithmic scheduling and GPS tracking in healthcare and elderly-care platforms, and argues that 'AI is eating the managers' while on-demand nursing firms erode patient care and social protections. Qualitative and normative rather than econometric; complements Fairwork's Global South ratings with an AI-management angle.

title: The Algorithmic Human Manager: AI, Apps, and Workers in the Indian Gig Economy
authors: Omir Kumar, Krishnan Narayanan (Centre for Responsible AI, IIT Madras)
institution: Centre for Responsible AI (CeRAI), IIT Madras
verification: Executive summary read from the 54-page PDF 2026-11-05; full report not read.
relevance: India-focused, mixed-methods study of AI-mediated management of blue-collar gig workers (ride-sharing, delivery, home services), based on in-depth interviews with 16 gig workers and 21 key stakeholders within a social-justice framework. Workers experience the app as 'the manager' but believe humans behind the curtain make the real decisions, and report opaque task allocation, stage determination, pay structures and penalties beyond their control; stakeholders describe practices such as 'algorithmic cruelty' via manipulated incentives and deactivations without due process. The report situates findings in India's policy landscape (Code on Social Security 2020 not yet notified; state-level measures in Rajasthan, Karnataka, Jharkhand, Bihar and Telangana). Small qualitative sample, but rare primary evidence from the worker side in a major gig economy.

title: Exposure to Artificial Intelligence and Occupational Mobility: A Cross-Country Analysis
authors: Mauro Cazzaniga, Carlo Pizzinelli, Emma Rockall, Marina M. Tavares
institution: Economia LACEA Journal, vol. 24, issue 1, pp. 314-339 (authors affiliated with the IMF)
verification: Abstract and key findings read at origin (economia.lse.ac.uk) 2026-11-05. DOI 10.31389/eco.451.
relevance: Open-access study of workers' occupational transitions in Brazil and the UK, classifying jobs by AI exposure and complementarity (high-exposure/high-complementarity, high-exposure/low-complementarity, low-exposure). Over 85 percent of college-educated workers in both countries are in high-exposure occupations; the UK has 35 percent of employment in high-exposure/high-complementarity jobs versus 19 percent in Brazil, and college education raises the probability of moving into such jobs by 11.4 percentage points in Brazil versus 2.26 in the UK. Simulations suggest destroying all high-exposure/low-complementarity jobs would cut lifetime earnings by 27.9 percent for college and 31.7 percent for non-college workers in Brazil. Brazil's much higher quarterly occupational switching (33 percent versus 12 percent) and 42 percent informality are the key institutional differences; mobility data are survey-based and pre-date large-scale generative AI.

title: Interactions of Artificial Intelligence with India's Labour Market: Devising an AI-for-Labour Model using the Productivity, Inclusivity, and Entrepreneurship Framework
authors: Payal Malik, Nikita Jain
institution: ICRIER Prosus Centre for Internet and Digital Economy (Policy Brief No. 10)
verification: Abstract, authors and contents read from the 19-page PDF 2026-11-05; full brief not read.
relevance: Indian think-tank analysis of AI-labour interactions using national databases (KLEMS, PLFS and NCO classifications), grouping the economy into four structural categories and applying a productivity-inclusivity-entrepreneurship framework to sector-wise AI exposure and adjustment capacity. The authors conclude AI diffusion in India will be uneven: displacement risk is limited for now in employment-intensive, low-productivity sectors, but exclusion from AI-enabled productivity gains is the bigger concern; manufacturing can upgrade through servicification; knowledge-intensive services face augmentation requiring high-level skilling. Argues for a diffusion-first AI strategy built on skills, infrastructure and institutions. Desk-based synthesis rather than causal estimation.

title: South Asia Development Update, October 2025: Jobs, AI, and Trade — Chapter 2: Artificial Intelligence, Real Impact: Labor Market Implications of AI Adoption in South Asia
authors: World Bank
institution: World Bank (South Asia Development Update, DOI 10.1596/978-1-4648-2291-9)
verification: Chapter 2 text read from the open PDF bitstream 2026-11-05; Open Knowledge landing page confirmed the same day (publication dated 2025-10-07).
relevance: Flagship regional report chapter quantifying AI exposure in South Asia using occupation-level measures and job-listings data. Only 7 percent of South Asia's jobs are highly exposed to AI without complementarity (at automation risk), well below the 15 percent exposure in other emerging markets, while the 15 percent of workers in jobs with strong AI complementarities could see substantial productivity gains. Jobs requiring AI skills command a wage premium of nearly 30 percent relative to other white-collar jobs, and generative AI has already reduced monthly job listings by around 20 percent for the most exposed and most substitutable white-collar occupations, with largest losses in business services and IT among upper-middle-skilled and entry-level workers. Exposure estimates rest on US-derived task measures applied to the region, a limitation the report acknowledges.

title: Adoption of artificial intelligence in Spanish firms: an initial analysis based on the Banco de España Business Activity Survey
authors: Alejandro Fernández Cerezo, Ignacio Hidalgo, Mario Izquierdo
institution: Banco de España (Economic Bulletin, Analytical Article, 2025/Q2, article 06; DOI 10.53479/39725)
verification: Abstract and summary read via the RePEc listing 2026-11-05; the Banco de España article page itself was not fetched.
relevance: Central-bank survey evidence on AI adoption in Spain using the Banco de España Business Activity Survey (EBAE). Almost 20 percent of Spanish firms surveyed use AI systems — below comparable figures for Germany but above Italy — though most remain at the experimentation stage. Adoption is highest in technology services and among large, productive and young firms; the main barriers are lack of skilled labour, high implementation costs and data availability; uses concentrate on optimizing internal processes and marketing rather than automation or innovation. Notably, 80 percent of firms believe AI will not affect employment, and firms already using AI expect a positive employment impact.

title: Artificial intelligence in UK businesses: 2023 to 2026
authors: Office for National Statistics (Macroeconomic Insights team)
institution: Office for National Statistics (UK)
verification: Article read at origin (ons.gov.uk) 2026-11-05.
relevance: Official UK time series on business AI use, usable to benchmark adoption claims. AI use among UK businesses with 10 or more employees rose from roughly 12 percent in late 2023 to about 35 percent by June 2026, with 49 percent of firms with 250+ employees using AI versus 28 percent of firms with 0-9 employees. Large language models were the most used technology (18 percent), information and communication the leading industry (58 percent), and improving business operations the most common purpose (around 60 percent of users). Most adopting firms reported no headcount change (about 6 percent of medium-sized firms reported decreases), and 41 percent of businesses reported no adoption barriers.

title: Artificial intelligence adoption and productivity in Canadian firms
authors: Jiang Li (Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada), Huju Liu (Statistics Canada)
institution: Statistics Canada (Economic and Social Reports, catalogue 36-28-0001; DOI 10.25318/36280001202600400002-eng)
verification: Full article summary read at origin (statcan.gc.ca) 2026-11-05.
relevance: Official Canada-wide firm study linking the Canadian Survey on Business Conditions to productivity outcomes. 12.2 percent of Canadian firms used AI to produce goods or deliver services in 2025 — double the previous year's share — with a further 14.5 percent planning to adopt within 12 months. AI adopters show 16.8 percent higher labour productivity than non-adopters, but the premium falls to 10.2 percent controlling for pre-adoption productivity, and to a statistically insignificant 5.1 percent once complementary capabilities (R&D, cloud computing, data analytics, robotics, ICT training) are added; no significant link to short-term productivity growth. The authors conclude AI pays off only when embedded in broader digital-transformation strategies — a cautionary benchmark for headline adoption-productivity claims.

title: AI adoption in America: Who, what, and where
authors: Kristina McElheran, J. Frank Li, Erik Brynjolfsson, Zachary Kroff, Emin Dinlersoz, Lucia Foster, Nikolas Zolas
institution: Journal of Economics and Management Strategy (Census Annual Business Survey module; Stanford Digital Economy Lab)
verification: Publisher page (Wiley) returned HTTP 403 on 2026-11-05; summary read from the Stanford Digital Economy Lab publication page the same day. Journal version published in the Journal of Economics and Management Strategy, 2024.
relevance: The foundational peer-reviewed description of the US Census Bureau's first comprehensive AI module in the Annual Business Survey, covering about 850,000 firms with questions on five AI technologies (automated-guided vehicles, machine learning, machine vision, natural language processing, voice recognition). Fewer than 6 percent of firms used any measured AI technology in the 2018 reference period, but employment-weighted adoption exceeded 18 percent, showing concentration in large firms. Adoption clustered with cloud computing and robotics, was higher among young firms with venture funding and high-growth signals, and was geographically concentrated in a few superstar cities — the base dataset for much subsequent US firm-level AI research.

title: Singapore Digital Economy Report 2024/2025 (state of AI adoption chapter)
authors: Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA)
institution: Infocomm Media Development Authority, Singapore
verification: Executive summary and AI-adoption sections read from the 27-page PDF 2026-11-05.
relevance: Official Singapore statistics on enterprise and worker AI adoption, among the most granular national series in Asia. SME AI adoption tripled from 4.2 percent in 2023 to 14.5 percent in 2024, driven mainly by off-the-shelf generative AI tools, while non-SME adoption rose from 44.0 percent to 62.5 percent; the digital economy reached S$128.1 billion, 18.6 percent of GDP. A companion IMDA pulse survey found 73.8 percent of surveyed workers use AI tools at work, 85 percent of AI users reported productivity, time-saving or quality improvements, and the share of tech job postings requiring AI skills rose from 11 percent in 2019 to 14 percent in 2024. Based on IMDA's annual enterprise survey methodology, so self-reported.

title: Economic Growth under Transformative AI
authors: Philip Trammell, Anton Korinek
institution: NBER (Working Paper 31815); published in the Annual Review of Economics, vol. 18 (2026)
verification: Abstract read at origin (nber.org) 2026-11-05; revision date April 2026 and published-version pointer per NBER page.
relevance: The standard synthesis of growth models under transformative AI, reviewing what happens if machines can automate essentially all work. Robustly, full automation of production (machine self-replication) would dramatically raise growth rates and lower the labour share, breaking the Kaldor Facts; automating R&D (machine self-improvement) would accelerate the transformation but may not produce it alone. Wages — the product of exploding output and a plummeting labour share — may rise or fall depending on returns to scale, natural resources, and the direction of technical change. A framework paper rather than new empirics; useful as the map of AGI-growth modelling assumptions.

title: We Won't be Missed: Work and Growth in the AGI World
authors: Pascual Restrepo
institution: Yale University (prepared for the NBER conference volume The Economics of Transformative AI)
verification: Abstract and introduction read from the PDF 2026-11-05; full 39-page chapter not read. The author discloses membership of Anthropic's Economic Advisory Council since May 2025.
relevance: A formal model of long-run growth and wages once artificial general intelligence can perform all economically valuable work with compute. The author distinguishes bottleneck work (essential for growth) from supplementary work, and shows the economy eventually automates all bottleneck work, output becomes linear in compute and labour, growth is driven by compute expansion, wages converge to the opportunity cost of the compute needed to replicate human work, and the labour share of income converges to zero. Even post-AGI, positive wages persist for skills that save compute and for supplementary tasks left to humans. Pure theory with stark distributional implications; no data.

title: Miracle or Myth? Assessing the macroeconomic productivity gains from Artificial Intelligence
authors: Francesco Filippucci, Peter Gal, Matthias Schief
institution: OECD (Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 29)
verification: Abstract and key estimates read via the RePEc listing (ideas.repec.org) 2026-11-05; the OECD landing page returned only navigation content. DOI 10.1787/b524a072-en.
relevance: A micro-to-macro reconciliation of why AI productivity forecasts diverge: the authors combine micro-level performance-gain estimates with evidence on AI exposure and likely adoption rates, aggregating through a multi-sector general equilibrium model with input-output linkages over a 10-year horizon. Their central estimate is annual aggregate total-factor productivity growth from AI of 0.25-0.6 percentage points, rising to 0.4-0.9 percentage points for labour productivity. The paper analyzes the channels shaping gains (adoption speed, complementarities, reallocation) and highlights policy levers. The benchmark 'sober middle' scenario between boom and scepticism in the Solow-paradox debate.

title: AI innovation and the labor share in European regions
authors: Antonio Minniti, Klaus Prettner, Francesco Venturini
institution: European Economic Review, vol. 177, article 105043 (Elsevier)
verification: Abstract read via the RePEc listing 2026-11-05; ScienceDirect returned no usable content and SSRN returned HTTP 403 the same day. DOI 10.1016/j.euroecorev.2025.105043.
relevance: Peer-reviewed evidence that AI innovation shifts income from labour to capital within European regions, using regional data from 2000 onwards. Each doubling of regional AI innovation reduces the labour share by 0.5 to 1.6 percent, which the authors translate into a reduction of 0.09 to 0.31 percentage points from an average labour share of 52 percent attributable to AI. The technology harms high- and medium-skill workers most, mainly through wage compression, while AI-induced employment growth slightly offsets wage declines for low-skill workers. Effects are robust to excluding other regional development drivers and AI-market concentration; identification is correlational with fixed effects rather than experimental.

title: The Rise of Industrial AI in America: Microfoundations of the Productivity J-curve(s)
authors: Kristina McElheran (University of Toronto), Mu-Jeung Yang (University of Oklahoma), Zachary Kroff, Erik Brynjolfsson (Stanford University)
institution: US Census Bureau, Center for Economic Studies (CES Working Paper 25-27)
verification: Title page, abstract and introduction read from the 56-page PDF 2026-11-05; full paper not read.
relevance: Census working paper providing the causal micro-foundations for the AI productivity J-curve — the modern Solow paradox. Using two waves of large-scale data collected with the Census Bureau for 2017 and 2021 on AI in American manufacturing, the authors find short-term performance losses (harming productivity and profitability, raising work-in-progress inventory, robot investment and labour shedding) that precede longer-term gains, concentrated among older businesses and mitigated by growth-oriented strategies and within-firm spillovers. Abandonment of structured production-management practices accounts for roughly one-third of the short-run losses among older establishments, identifying a specific intangible-capital channel. Pre-2017 adopters exhibit stronger growth conditional on survival; results are manufacturing-specific and cover the pre-generative-AI wave.
